rationale: New admissions with sepsis are unstable with unpredictable outcomes, so the initial assessment including vital signs is an RN function. Routine vital signs on stable patients may be delegated to the UAP.

stem: Which of the five rights of delegation is violated when the RN assigns a dressing change to a UAP who was never trained in sterile technique?
options: The right task, because dressing changes are never delegable
The right direction, because the RN gave clear instructions
The right person, because the delegatee lacks competency for the task
The right supervision, because the RN stayed on the unit
rationale: The right person requires the delegatee to be competent in the task. Additionally, wound care is generally not within UAP scope at all, but the specific failure here is assigning a task to someone without verified competency.

stem: A patient fell on the unit and hit his head. Who should perform the post-fall assessment?
options: The RN, because post-fall assessment requires neurologic evaluation and clinical judgment
The UAP, who witnessed the fall
The LPN, who can check vital signs and report
The charge nurse's designee, regardless of licensure
rationale: Post-fall assessment, especially with head strike, requires RN neurologic assessment and decision-making about escalation. Others contribute observations and vital signs, but the evaluation belongs to the RN.

stem: A stable patient needs a Foley catheter inserted per provider order. Which statement is correct?
options: Only the RN may insert any urinary catheter
The LPN may insert the Foley catheter in a stable patient where state scope permits
The UAP may insert the catheter after training
The LPN may also order the catheter removed when output improves
rationale: Routine Foley insertion in a stable patient is within LPN scope in most states. UAPs do not perform catheter insertion, and decisions about removal require RN assessment and provider direction.

stem: The RN asks the UAP to sit with a patient on 1:1 observation for suicide precautions. Which instruction is essential?
options: Assess the patient's mood every hour
Stay with the patient continuously, maintain a safe environment, and report any concerning behavior immediately
Decide when the patient no longer needs observation
Counsel the patient on coping strategies
rationale: One-to-one observation is an appropriate UAP task focused on continuous presence, safety, and reporting. Assessing mood, discontinuing precautions, and counseling require licensed-nurse and provider judgment.

stem: A patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) pump is ordered for post-op pain. Who should program the initial PCA settings?
options: The LPN, who will be monitoring the patient
The RN, because PCA programming requires assessment and carries high overdose risk
The UAP, under the RN's direct supervision
The patient, who controls the demand button
rationale: Programming a PCA pump is an RN function due to the risks of opioid overdose and the assessment required. The patient uses the demand button, and the LPN may monitor the stable patient per policy, but initial programming is RN-only.

stem: A newly diagnosed hypertensive patient needs teaching about low-sodium eating. The RN is tied up with an emergency. What is the best plan?
options: The LPN provides the full initial teaching now
The UAP teaches the diet using the handout
The RN provides the initial teaching when available; the LPN may share the printed diet handout meanwhile
Skip the teaching and document that the patient refused
rationale: Initial teaching requires the RN even when busy; the emergency takes priority and teaching is rescheduled. Others may provide written materials, but the RN must still perform and evaluate the teaching.

stem: Discharge planning for a complex patient needing home wound care and physical therapy should be coordinated by whom?
options: The UAP, who knows the patient's daily routine best
The LPN, who can arrange the referrals independently
The RN, who assesses needs, arranges referrals, and evaluates the plan
The case manager alone, without nursing input
rationale: Discharge planning requires RN assessment of the patient's needs, coordination of referrals, and evaluation. The RN collaborates with case management but retains the nursing assessment and planning role.

stem: An LPN is asked to reinforce teaching about incentive spirometer use to a stable post-op patient. Is this appropriate?
options: No, only RNs may discuss incentive spirometers
Yes, reinforcing previously taught material is within LPN scope
Yes, and the LPN may also evaluate the patient's technique as the formal evaluation
No, the UAP should do the reinforcement instead
rationale: Reinforcement of teaching the RN already provided is appropriate for the LPN. Formal evaluation of learning outcomes, however, remains an RN function.

stem: Which feeding task may the UAP perform?
options: Feed a patient with new dysphagia after a stroke
Decide the patient is too tired to eat and skip the meal
Assess the patient's swallowing before the meal
Feed a stable patient without swallowing precautions and report intake
rationale: Feeding a stable patient without aspiration risk is a routine UAP task. New dysphagia requires RN assessment of swallowing, and decisions to skip meals require licensed-nurse judgment.

stem: The RN delegates wound assessment to the LPN. Which statement is correct?
options: Assessment may not be delegated; the LPN may collect wound data but the RN performs the assessment
Assessment is delegable when the LPN is experienced
The LPN's data collection counts as the assessment
The RN may delegate assessment if she co-signs the note
rationale: Assessment is a non-delegable nursing function. The LPN may gather objective data such as wound measurements and report them, but interpreting the data and drawing conclusions is the RN's assessment role.

stem: A patient with diabetes has a blood glucose of 42 mg/dL and is sweaty and confused. Who should direct the immediate response?
options: The UAP, who found the patient
The LPN, who can follow the hypoglycemia protocol alone
The dietary aide, who can bring juice
The RN, because symptomatic hypoglycemia requires rapid assessment and intervention decisions
rationale: Symptomatic hypoglycemia is an urgent change in condition requiring RN assessment and direction of treatment. Others may assist with specific tasks such as bringing juice, but the RN leads the clinical response.

stem: A stable patient is ordered a routine bladder scan for retention. Which statement is correct?
options: Only the RN may operate the bladder scanner
The UAP may perform the scan after watching once
The LPN may perform the bladder scan and report the volume to the RN
The LPN may catheterize based on the result without notifying the RN
rationale: Operating the bladder scanner and reporting the result is within LPN scope. Interpreting the result in context and deciding on catheterization require RN judgment and a provider order.

stem: Which transport situation is appropriate for the UAP?
options: Transporting an unstable patient on a norepinephrine infusion
Transporting a patient with a new chest tube to CT
Transporting a stable patient to radiology for a routine x-ray
Transporting a laboring patient to the delivery room
rationale: Transport of stable patients for routine tests is an appropriate UAP task. Unstable patients, vasoactive infusions, new chest tubes, and laboring patients require licensed-nurse monitoring during transport.

stem: A patient needs total parenteral nutrition (TPN) initiated through a central line. Who should manage the TPN?
options: The LPN, who hangs tube feedings regularly
The UAP, who can report the infusion rate
The RN, because TPN requires complex assessment of glucose, fluids, and line complications
The LPN, as long as pharmacy premixed the bag
rationale: TPN management involves monitoring for hyperglycemia, fluid shifts, and central line complications, requiring RN-level assessment. Hanging enteral feedings does not qualify an LPN for parenteral nutrition management.

stem: A patient asks the LPN detailed questions about the risks of a newly prescribed anticoagulant. What should the LPN do?
options: Provide a full risk-benefit analysis from her own experience
Tell the patient only the provider can discuss medications
Answer general information within her knowledge and refer detailed risk questions to the RN
Have the UAP look up the answers online
rationale: The LPN may share general medication information and reinforce RN teaching, but detailed risk counseling requiring assessment of the patient's understanding belongs to the RN. Refusing to discuss anything is unhelpful; referring appropriately is correct.

stem: A patient is being transferred to the ICU for worsening sepsis. Who should give the handoff report?
options: The UAP, who has been sitting with the patient
The LPN, to save the RN time
The RN, because handoff of an unstable patient requires RN-to-RN communication of assessments
The unit secretary, who has the chart ready
rationale: Handoff of an unstable patient requires the RN to communicate assessments, trends, and pending issues nurse-to-nurse. Others may assist with logistics, but the clinical handoff is an RN responsibility.

stem: An LPN is floated to a medical-surgical unit and assigned stable patients. Which additional task may she take on?
options: Take the newly admitted chest pain patient for the team
Initiate the blood transfusion ordered for her patient
Perform the admission assessments for her team
Administer scheduled oral and subcutaneous medications to her stable patients
rationale: Floating does not change scope: the LPN may give routine medications to stable patients. New unstable admissions, transfusions, and initial assessments remain RN functions regardless of the unit.

stem: A patient with lymphoma is scheduled for his first IV chemotherapy infusion on the medical-surgical unit. The LPN offers to hang the chemotherapy. What is the correct response?
options: Chemotherapy administration requires an RN with chemotherapy competency; the LPN may not hang it
The LPN may hang it since the pharmacy prepared the bag
The UAP may hang it while the LPN monitors
The LPN may hang it after the RN verifies the order
rationale: Antineoplastic administration requires specialized RN competency because of vesicant risks, hypersensitivity, and dosing complexity. Pharmacy preparation does not make the administration task delegable to an LPN.

stem: A stable patient has a peripheral IV of normal saline running. The LPN asks whether she may start a new IV on another patient whose IV infiltrated. What should the RN say?
options: IV insertion is generally an RN function; the RN will start the new line
The LPN may start the IV since she monitors infusions
The UAP may attempt the insertion with coaching
The LPN may start it because the patient is stable
rationale: Peripheral IV insertion requires assessment of vein selection, infection risk, and complications, and is an RN function in most states. Monitoring an existing infusion is within LPN scope, but initiating access is not.

stem: A patient is receiving her first dose of IV vancomycin. Fifteen minutes in, she reports itching and flushing. Who should assess and respond?
options: The LPN, who hung the piggyback
The UAP, who can slow the infusion rate
The patient, who can decide whether to continue
The RN, because first-dose reactions require RN assessment and intervention decisions
rationale: First-dose IV antibiotic reactions such as red man syndrome require the RN to assess severity, decide whether to slow or stop the infusion, and notify the provider. Rate changes based on assessment are RN decisions.

stem: The RN asks the UAP to stay with a confused patient while the RN assesses another patient. The UAP leaves to answer a call light. Which principle was breached?
options: The right task, because sitting with patients is never delegable
The right person, because UAPs cannot observe confused patients
The right supervision and direction, because the UAP left a safety-critical assignment without coverage
The right circumstance, because call lights take priority
rationale: Staying with a confused patient is a delegable safety task, and the UAP was the right person. The breach is supervision and direction: the delegatee must not abandon the assigned task, and the RN must ensure continuous coverage.

stem: A patient with a new chest tube after pneumothorax is stable. The LPN asks to 'check the chest tube system.' What is within her scope?
options: Strip the chest tube to maintain patency
Decide when the chest tube can be removed
Observe and report the drainage amount, color, and tidaling to the RN
Adjust the suction level based on the air leak
rationale: The LPN may observe and report objective chest tube data. Stripping tubes, changing suction, and removal decisions require RN assessment and provider orders because of the risk of tension pneumothorax and lung injury.

stem: The RN delegates hourly rounding to the UAP. During rounds the UAP notices a patient's surgical dressing is saturated with bright red blood. What should the UAP do?
options: Reinforce the dressing with additional gauze
Notify the RN immediately without removing or changing the dressing
Remove the dressing to assess the wound
Document the finding and finish the remaining rounds first
rationale: The UAP's role is to observe and promptly report abnormal findings. Changing or removing dressings is wound care outside UAP scope, and delaying the report to finish rounds endangers the patient.

stem: A patient on telemetry shows a new run of ventricular tachycardia on the monitor. Who should assess the patient and initiate the response?
options: The monitor technician, who saw it first
The LPN, who is closest to the room
The RN, who correlates the rhythm with the patient's clinical status and acts
The UAP, who can check whether the patient is awake
rationale: Rhythm interpretation tied to patient assessment and emergency response requires RN judgment. Others report what they see, but the RN assesses the patient, determines stability, and leads the intervention.

stem: A patient being discharged on a new anticoagulant asks the LPN how long to take it and what to do if she misses a dose. What should the LPN do?
options: Give her best estimate based on other patients
Tell the patient to skip the medication entirely
Reinforce what the RN taught and refer unanswered questions back to the RN
Have the UAP print general internet articles
rationale: The LPN may reinforce teaching already provided by the RN but should not independently counsel on a new high-risk medication. Referring detailed questions to the RN protects the patient from inaccurate guidance.

stem: A norepinephrine infusion is ordered for a hypotensive septic patient. Who should titrate the infusion?
options: The RN, because vasoactive titration requires continuous hemodynamic assessment
The LPN, following the written titration parameters
The UAP, reporting the blood pressure each hour
The LPN, if an RN is available by phone
rationale: Vasoactive infusions demand ongoing RN assessment of perfusion, blood pressure trends, and adverse effects. Written parameters guide but never replace the clinical judgment titration requires.

stem: An LPN is caring for a stable patient with an epidural infusion for post-op pain. Which task may the LPN perform?
options: Administer an epidural bolus for breakthrough pain
Remove the epidural catheter when the order is written
Adjust the epidural infusion rate
Monitor the patient's pain level and report changes to the RN
rationale: Epidural management, including boluses, rate changes, and catheter removal, is RN-only due to risks of respiratory depression and hypotension. The LPN may monitor and report the patient's pain and vital signs.

stem: A nurse discovers a stage 3 pressure injury on a newly admitted patient. Who should perform the initial wound assessment and staging?
options: The LPN, who will be doing the dressing changes
The UAP, who found the redness
The RN, because initial wound assessment and staging require RN clinical judgment
The wound care nurse only, so the RN should not assess
rationale: Initial assessment and staging of a pressure injury is an RN function that drives the care plan. The LPN may perform subsequent dressing changes per the plan, and specialty consultation supports but does not replace the RN's assessment.

stem: Which task can the RN safely delegate to a competent UAP?
options: Evaluating the patient's response to a new diuretic
Measuring intake and output for a stable post-op patient
Teaching the patient about fluid restrictions
Assessing the patient's edema
rationale: Intake and output measurement is a routine, predictable task appropriate for a UAP. Evaluating diuretic response, teaching fluid restrictions, and assessing edema all require licensed-nurse judgment.

stem: A family asks about the risks and benefits of their father's proposed surgery to give informed consent. Who should address this?
options: The LPN, who can explain the surgical risks
The UAP, who has time to sit with the family
The provider, who obtains informed consent; the RN may witness the signature
The RN, who may obtain the consent independently
rationale: Informed consent requires the provider to explain risks, benefits, and alternatives. Nurses witness the signature and verify understanding, but explaining surgical risks to obtain consent is the provider's role.

stem: A stable patient needs a routine pre-op shower with chlorhexidine the night before surgery. Which is appropriate?
options: The UAP may shave the surgical site with a razor
The UAP may mark the surgical site
The UAP may assist with the chlorhexidine shower per the pre-op checklist
The UAP may verify the consent is signed
rationale: Assisting with the ordered pre-op shower is a routine UAP task. Site marking and consent verification require licensed or provider roles, and razors are avoided in surgical prep per policy.

stem: A stable patient with COPD needs a routine nebulizer treatment. Which statement is correct?
options: Only the RN may administer any respiratory treatment
The UAP may administer it after one demonstration
The LPN may administer the scheduled nebulizer treatment to this stable patient
The LPN may also change the ordered medication dose
rationale: Scheduled nebulizer treatments for stable patients are within LPN scope in most states. Changing doses requires a provider order and RN assessment, and UAPs do not administer medications including nebulizers.

stem: A patient returns from a procedure with a new central line. Who should perform the initial central line assessment and dressing verification?
options: The LPN, who will monitor the line
The UAP, who can check that it is labeled
The RN, because central line assessment requires evaluation for complications
The transporter, who brought the patient back
rationale: Initial assessment of a new central line for placement complications, patency, and dressing integrity is an RN function. LPNs may monitor established lines per policy, but the initial assessment belongs to the RN.

stem: The RN taught a heart failure patient about daily weights and fluid limits yesterday. Today the LPN is assigned to the patient. What may the LPN do?
options: Evaluate whether the teaching was effective and document mastery
Develop a new teaching plan for low-sodium cooking
Ask the patient to explain back the weight and fluid plan as reinforcement
Cancel the teaching because the patient seems to understand
rationale: The LPN may reinforce teaching and use teach-back to check recall, reporting results to the RN. Formal evaluation of learning and developing new teaching plans are RN functions.

stem: Which IV medication task is within LPN scope in most states?
options: Pushing IV ondansetron for nausea
Mixing IV vancomycin in the medication room
Monitoring a stable patient receiving a premixed IV antibiotic piggyback
Programming a new PCA pump
rationale: Monitoring an established piggyback infusion is generally within LPN scope, while IV push, admixture preparation, and PCA programming require RN practice. State laws vary, so the nurse must know her own practice act.

stem: The RN is pulled to an emergency and asks the LPN to 'keep an eye on' her unstable patient. What is the problem?
options: The RN is attempting to delegate assessment and monitoring of an unstable patient, which cannot be delegated
LPNs cannot monitor any patients
The RN should have asked the UAP instead
There is no problem; teamwork covers this
rationale: An unstable patient requires RN assessment and cannot be handed to the LPN as a delegation. The RN must arrange RN coverage for the unstable patient rather than delegating the assessment responsibility.

stem: A stable patient needs routine suctioning of oral secretions with a Yankauer. Which staff may perform it?
options: Only the RN may perform any suctioning
The UAP may perform deep tracheal suctioning
The LPN may perform oral suctioning on this stable patient
The LPN may also perform deep nasotracheal suctioning independently
rationale: Oral suctioning with a Yankauer on a stable patient is within LPN scope. Deep or nasotracheal suctioning requires greater assessment and is generally an RN function.

stem: Which documentation task is appropriate for the UAP?
options: Documenting her assessment of the patient's lung sounds
Documenting the effectiveness of pain medication
Documenting the intake and output amounts she measured
Writing the nursing progress note for the shift
rationale: UAPs document the objective data they collect, such as intake, output, and vital signs. Assessments, evaluations of interventions, and progress notes require licensed-nurse judgment.

stem: A provider writes an order for a new blood pressure medication. The patient asks how it works. Who should provide the initial medication teaching?
options: The LPN, who will administer the first dose
The RN, who assesses learning needs and evaluates understanding
The UAP, who delivers the medication cup
The pharmacist, who cannot teach patients
rationale: Initial medication teaching requires RN assessment of learning needs and evaluation of comprehension. The pharmacist is an excellent resource and often co-teaches, but the nursing teaching process belongs to the RN.

stem: An LPN floats to the telemetry unit for the first time. Which assignment is appropriate?
options: The new chest pain admission for initial assessment
Titration of a diltiazem infusion
Independent management of a patient in new-onset atrial fibrillation with hypotension
Stable telemetry patients with predictable outcomes, with RN resource available
rationale: Floating does not expand scope: the LPN takes stable patients with predictable outcomes. New unstable admissions and infusion titration require RN practice, and the float nurse needs an identified RN resource.

stem: A patient has a heavily draining, foul-smelling wound with suspected infection. The LPN is asked to change the dressing. What should happen first?
options: The LPN changes it and decides on a new dressing type
The RN assesses the wound first, then the LPN may do subsequent changes per the updated plan
The UAP changes it to save time
The dressing is left unchanged until the provider rounds
rationale: A deteriorating or infected wound needs RN assessment to update the plan before routine changes continue. The LPN then performs subsequent changes per the revised plan and reports changes.

stem: Which task may the UAP perform for a patient in restraints?
options: Assess circulation in the restrained limbs
Perform safety checks such as offering fluids and toileting, and report observations
Decide the restraints can be removed
Apply the restraints initially
rationale: UAPs may perform safety checks and report observations for restrained patients. Applying restraints, assessing circulation, and discontinuing restraints require licensed-nurse and provider involvement.

stem: A post-op patient suddenly becomes diaphoretic, tachycardic, and confused. The UAP reports this to the LPN. What should the LPN do?
options: Assess the patient fully and manage the situation independently
Recheck vital signs in 30 minutes to see if it passes
Notify the RN immediately so the RN can assess this acute change
Give the patient juice in case it is low blood sugar
rationale: An acute change in condition must be escalated to the RN promptly for assessment. The LPN reports findings and may assist, but analyzing and managing the acute change is the RN's role.

stem: A patient needs IV potassium 20 mEq in 1 liter of saline over 8 hours. Who should verify the rate calculation and initiate the infusion?
options: The LPN, since the pharmacy premixed the bag
The UAP, who can set the pump
The RN, because electrolyte infusions require RN assessment of cardiac and renal status
The LPN, because potassium is a routine rider
rationale: IV potassium carries risks of cardiac arrhythmia and requires RN assessment of renal function, EKG, and infusion rate. Premixed bags do not remove the assessment requirement.

stem: The charge nurse overhears an RN telling a UAP to 'decide which patients need turning tonight.' What should the charge nurse do?
options: Praise the RN for empowering the UAP
Document the UAP's good judgment
Reassign the turning schedule to the LPN to decide
Intervene, because prioritizing and planning care cannot be delegated to the UAP
rationale: Planning and prioritizing care are RN functions. The RN may delegate the physical task of turning specific patients, but deciding who needs turning requires nursing assessment.

stem: Which statement about LPNs and blood glucose management is correct?
options: The LPN may independently manage an insulin infusion
The LPN may administer scheduled insulin per order and report results to the RN
The LPN may not perform any glucose-related tasks
The LPN may diagnose hypoglycemia and treat it without notifying the RN
rationale: Scheduled insulin administration per order with reporting is within LPN scope. Insulin infusions require RN management, and the LPN must communicate abnormal findings rather than managing them independently.

stem: A patient with a new ileostomy is tearful and overwhelmed. The LPN asks to take over the teaching. What is the best response?
options: The RN continues the initial teaching, addressing the emotional response, with the LPN reinforcing later
The LPN takes over since she is good with ostomies
The UAP sits with the patient instead of teaching
Teaching is postponed indefinitely
rationale: New ostomy teaching involves psychosocial assessment and adaptation, requiring RN judgment. The RN leads the initial teaching and evaluation, and the LPN reinforces once the RN has established the plan.

stem: Which activity requires the RN rather than the LPN?
options: Administering a scheduled oral pain medication
Reporting the patient's stated pain score
Reinforcing the use of relaxation techniques
Evaluating whether the patient's pain management plan is effective
rationale: Evaluation of plan effectiveness is an RN function in the nursing process. Administering scheduled medications, reporting stated scores, and reinforcing techniques are within LPN scope.

stem: A stable patient rings for help to the bathroom. The UAP is busy with another patient. What should the UAP do?
options: Tell the patient to wait indefinitely
Leave the current patient unattended to rush over
Ensure the patient is safe, notify the nurse, and arrange timely coverage
Ignore the light because toileting is the RN's job
rationale: The UAP must not abandon her current patient or ignore the call light. Ensuring safety, communicating the need, and arranging coverage maintains safe delegation and teamwork.

stem: An LPN asks to administer IV push furosemide because 'it is just a diuretic.' What is the correct teaching?
options: IV push administration is outside LPN scope regardless of the drug's familiarity
Familiar drugs are exempt from the IV push restriction
The LPN may push it if the RN watches
The UAP may push it if the LPN draws it up
rationale: Scope boundaries are based on the route and its risks, not familiarity with the drug. IV push requires rapid assessment of response and is RN-only in most states; observation does not expand scope.

stem: A stable patient with a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) needs a dressing change. Who should perform it?
options: The LPN, since it is just a dressing change
The UAP, using sterile gloves
The patient, after instruction
The RN, because PICC dressing changes require central line competency
rationale: PICC lines are central lines, and their dressing changes require RN central-line competency and assessment for infection. Peripheral IV site care may be within LPN scope, but central lines are not.

stem: The LPN notes increasing redness and warmth around a surgical wound during a routine dressing change. What should she do?
options: Change to a different dressing type she thinks is better
Complete the ordered dressing change and report the findings to the RN promptly
Stop the dressing change and leave the wound open
Document the redness and mention it tomorrow
rationale: The LPN performs the ordered change and promptly reports signs of infection. Changing the treatment plan independently or delaying the report would exceed scope and endanger the patient.

stem: When delegating to the UAP, which direction from the RN is most effective?
options: Specific, patient-centered instructions with clear expectations and timeframes
A general request to 'help out on the unit'
Written orders only, with no verbal communication
Delegation through another UAP
rationale: Effective delegation requires clear, specific direction: what to do, for whom, when, and what to report. Vague requests and indirect communication increase the risk of missed or unsafe care.

stem: A patient with heart failure gained 2 kg overnight and has new crackles. Who should evaluate this change?
options: The UAP, who obtained the weight
The RN, because new symptoms require RN assessment and care-plan revision
The LPN, who can adjust the diuretic
The dietary aide, who controls the sodium
rationale: New crackles with rapid weight gain signal worsening heart failure requiring RN assessment, provider notification, and plan revision. The UAP and LPN contribute data, but evaluation and decisions are RN functions.

stem: Which specimen collection may the UAP perform?
options: A routine stool specimen for occult blood testing
An arterial blood gas specimen
A sterile wound culture
A blood culture from a central line
rationale: Routine noninvasive specimens such as stool samples are appropriate for UAPs. Arterial sticks, sterile wound cultures, and central line cultures require licensed-nurse skill and assessment.

stem: An LPN is asked to perform the admission assessment on a stable elective surgical patient. Is this appropriate?
options: Yes, because the patient is stable and the surgery is elective
Yes, if the LPN has done admissions before
No, because only the charge nurse does admissions
No, initial admission assessments are an RN function even when the patient is stable
rationale: The initial comprehensive admission assessment establishes the baseline care plan and requires RN judgment regardless of stability. The LPN may collect admission data such as vital signs and history details for the RN to synthesize.

stem: Which statement about UAPs and patient teaching is correct?
options: UAPs may teach new medications using handouts
UAPs do not perform patient teaching; they may share general comfort measures and refer questions to the nurse
UAPs may teach wound care to families
UAPs may evaluate whether teaching was understood
rationale: Teaching requires assessment and evaluation that UAPs are not educated or licensed to perform. UAPs support care with comfort measures and promptly refer clinical questions to licensed staff.

stem: A patient is receiving a continuous heparin infusion and the aPTT is supratherapeutic with oozing at the IV site. Who should respond?
options: The LPN, who can stop the infusion independently
The RN, who assesses bleeding risk and collaborates on the plan
The UAP, who noticed the oozing
The LPN, following the protocol without RN input
rationale: Supratherapeutic anticoagulation with bleeding requires RN assessment, possible infusion adjustment per protocol, and provider notification. Stopping or adjusting based on assessment is an RN decision.

stem: A confused patient pulls out his IV. The LPN restarts the assessment and the UAP holds pressure. Who decides whether to reinsert the IV and what type of access is needed?
options: The UAP, who held pressure
The LPN, who assessed the site
The patient, who refused the IV
The RN, who assesses the patient's needs and determines the plan for access
rationale: Deciding on reinsertion, access type, and alternatives after an adverse event requires RN assessment and planning. The team assists with tasks, but the clinical decision belongs to the RN.

stem: A new RN delegates morning blood glucose checks to a UAP who was validated last month. The patient is stable. Which right of delegation still needs attention?
options: The right task, because glucose checks are never delegable
The right person, because last month's validation expired
The right supervision, ensuring the RN reviews results and is available for problems
The right circumstance, because mornings are too busy
rationale: The task, person, and circumstance are appropriate here. The new RN must still provide supervision: reviewing results, following up on abnormal values, and remaining available — supervision is ongoing, not a one-time check.

stem: Which medication administration is outside LPN scope in most states?
options: Oral acetaminophen for a stable patient
Subcutaneous enoxaparin per protocol
Intramuscular vitamin B12 injection
IV push hydromorphone for breakthrough pain
rationale: IV push medications are outside LPN scope in most states due to rapid onset and assessment needs. Oral, subcutaneous, and intramuscular medications for stable patients are within LPN scope.

stem: The RN asks the UAP to check on a patient every 15 minutes after a fall. Which is the UAP's appropriate role?
options: Perform the neurologic assessments each visit
Decide when the frequent checks can stop
Document the neurologic findings
Perform the frequent safety checks and report any changes immediately
rationale: Frequent safety checks and reporting are appropriate UAP tasks. Neurologic assessment, deciding to discontinue checks, and documenting assessment findings are licensed-nurse functions.

stem: A patient has a small skin tear on the forearm covered with a simple adhesive bandage. Who may change it?
options: The UAP, since it is only a bandage
Only the provider may change any dressing
The LPN may also apply steri-strips to close the tear
The LPN may change the simple dressing per the plan; the UAP may not perform wound care
rationale: Even simple wound care is outside UAP scope. The LPN may change simple dressings per the established plan, but wound closure decisions require RN or provider assessment.

stem: A patient with pneumonia has increasing oxygen requirements and new confusion. Who should be assigned?
options: An LPN with a stable assignment to add this patient
A UAP for frequent monitoring
A new graduate RN without a preceptor
An RN, because the patient is unstable with changing needs
rationale: Deteriorating pneumonia with new confusion is unstable and requires RN assessment and management. Adding an unstable patient to an LPN assignment or relying on UAP monitoring is unsafe.

stem: Which statement about LPNs and blood transfusions is correct?
options: LPNs may hang blood if an RN stays in the room
LPNs do not initiate or monitor blood transfusions; this is an RN function
LPNs may monitor the second unit after the RN starts the first
UAPs may take transfusion vital signs instead of the RN
rationale: Blood transfusion initiation and monitoring require RN assessment for reactions throughout the infusion. Presence of an RN does not transfer the assessment responsibility, and transfusion vital signs require licensed-nurse interpretation.

stem: An LPN is caring for a patient with a new ileostomy. Which task is appropriate for the LPN?
options: Perform the initial pouching and stoma assessment
Teach the patient to change the appliance independently
Empty and measure the ileostomy output and report the amounts
Decide the patient is ready for discharge
rationale: Emptying and measuring output with reporting is within LPN scope. Initial pouching, stoma assessment, teaching independence, and discharge readiness require RN judgment.

stem: A diabetic patient asks the UAP why his feet must be checked daily. What should the UAP do?
options: Explain the general reason briefly if known, and refer detailed teaching to the nurse
Provide complete diabetic foot-care teaching
Tell the patient foot checks are unnecessary
Refuse to answer any patient questions
rationale: UAPs may share simple general information but must refer teaching that requires assessment to the nurse. Providing full teaching or refusing all questions are both incorrect.

stem: The RN delegates a dressing change to the LPN and a bed bath to the UAP for the same patient. Which statement is correct?
options: Both delegations are appropriate if each task matches the delegatee's scope and competency
The RN cannot delegate to two people for one patient
The LPN cannot accept delegation from the RN
The UAP cannot care for a patient with a wound
rationale: RNs may delegate different tasks to different team members as long as each task is within that person's scope and competency. The RN retains accountability and must supervise both.

stem: Who should conduct the initial pain assessment for a patient admitted with sickle cell crisis?
options: The LPN, who can use the 0-to-10 scale
The UAP, who can ask the number
The RN, because complex pain assessment requires RN judgment
The previous nurse's note, which already has a score
rationale: Sickle cell crisis pain assessment involves history, prior regimens, and psychosocial factors requiring RN judgment. A number alone is data; the comprehensive assessment is the RN's role.

stem: Which activity is outside UAP scope?
options: Assisting a stable patient with ambulation
Measuring vital signs on stable patients
Removing a patient's peripheral IV catheter
Reporting a patient's complaint of nausea
rationale: IV catheter removal requires assessment for complications and is a licensed-nurse task. Ambulation, routine vital signs, and reporting symptoms are appropriate UAP activities.

stem: A stable patient needs a routine intramuscular vitamin B12 injection. Which is correct?
options: Only the RN may give any injection
The UAP may give it after training
The LPN must have the RN push the plunger
The LPN may administer the IM injection to this stable patient
rationale: Intramuscular injections are within LPN scope in most states. UAPs do not administer medications, and RN co-administration is not required for routine IM injections within scope.

stem: A patient with severe nausea needs IV push ondansetron now. The RN is in another patient's room. What should the LPN do?
options: Notify the RN to administer the IV push medication
Administer the IV push since the patient is suffering
Have the UAP give it under observation
Document that the medication was refused
rationale: IV push medications remain RN-only even when the RN is busy or the patient is uncomfortable. The LPN's correct action is to notify the RN rather than exceed scope.

stem: Who should assess a new diabetic foot ulcer discovered on admission?
options: The RN, who stages the ulcer and initiates the care plan
The LPN, during the routine dressing change
The UAP, who noticed the odor
The podiatrist, so nursing need not assess
rationale: Initial assessment and staging of a new ulcer is an RN function that drives referrals and the care plan. Others report findings, but the nursing assessment belongs to the RN.

stem: An RN delegates vital signs to a UAP for four stable patients. One patient's blood pressure is markedly elevated. What must the RN do?
options: Have the UAP recheck it in an hour
Assess the patient directly and determine the appropriate response
Document the UAP's finding without follow-up
Ask the LPN to decide whether to notify the provider
rationale: Abnormal findings from delegated tasks require RN follow-up assessment. The RN must evaluate the patient, decide on interventions, and determine whether to notify the provider.

stem: A patient is admitted for observation after a transient ischemic attack. Who performs the initial neurologic assessment?
options: The UAP, using the NIH stroke scale handout
The RN, because baseline neurologic assessment requires RN judgment
The LPN, who can follow the checklist
The ED nurse's report, which replaces the assessment
rationale: Baseline neurologic assessment on admission requires RN performance and interpretation, even with a checklist. Handoff reports supplement but never replace the receiving RN's own assessment.

stem: Which task is appropriate for the LPN caring for a stable post-op patient?
options: Clear the patient for discharge
Reinforce the RN's teaching about deep breathing and coughing
Interpret the morning chest x-ray
Discontinue the IV without an order
rationale: Reinforcing taught content is within LPN scope. Discharge decisions, diagnostic interpretation, and discontinuing therapies without orders require RN or provider judgment.

stem: A patient asks the RN whether she can stop her antibiotic because she feels better. What is the RN's best response?
options: Tell her to do whatever she prefers
Assess her understanding, explain why completing the course matters, and evaluate her response
Have the UAP convince her to continue
Document noncompliance and move on
rationale: Medication teaching requires the RN to assess understanding, provide education, and evaluate the patient's decision. Dismissing the question or delegating persuasion to the UAP abdicates the teaching role.

stem: Which task requires the RN instead of the UAP?
options: Assessing a patient's swallowing before the first meal after a stroke
Delivering the meal tray to the bedside
Assisting a stable patient with eating
Reporting that the patient ate 50 percent of the meal
rationale: Swallowing assessment after stroke requires RN evaluation for aspiration risk before any oral intake. Tray delivery, assisting stable patients, and reporting intake are appropriate UAP tasks.

stem: A patient is ordered the first dose of IV piperacillin-tazobactam for a new infection. The LPN offers to hang the piggyback since she is free. What should the charge nurse decide?
options: The LPN may hang it because it is a premixed piggyback
The RN should administer the first dose, because new-drug reactions require RN assessment
The UAP may hang it while the LPN observes
The LPN may hang it if the patient has had penicillin before
rationale: First doses of IV medications carry allergy and reaction risks requiring RN assessment and readiness to intervene. Subsequent doses in a stable patient may fall within LPN scope per state law, but the first dose is an RN function.

stem: The UAP finds a diabetic patient sweaty, pale, and difficult to arouse. The UAP is validated in fingerstick technique. What should the UAP do?
options: Perform the fingerstick and give juice based on the result
Recheck in 15 minutes to see if the patient improves
Stay with the patient and notify the RN immediately for assessment
Help the patient to the bathroom in case it is unrelated
rationale: An unresponsive, symptomatic patient is unstable and requires immediate RN assessment. The UAP's role is continuous presence and prompt notification, not independent testing or treatment decisions.

stem: The RN is assigning a patient who needs frequent neurologic checks after a fall with head strike. Which assignment decision is correct?
options: Assign the patient to the LPN for the neuro checks
Assign the UAP to do the neuro checks and report
Assign any available staff since checks are routine
Assign the patient to an RN, because serial neurologic checks are assessments
rationale: Serial neurologic assessments after head strike require RN interpretation of subtle changes. Data collection alone is not the issue here; the checks themselves are assessments that cannot be delegated to LPNs or UAPs.

stem: The charge nurse is assigning six patients among an RN, an LPN, and a UAP. One patient is 4 hours post-op with dropping hemoglobin and tachycardia. Who should be assigned this patient?
options: The LPN, who is experienced with post-op patients
The UAP, for frequent vital-sign monitoring
The new graduate RN, for the learning experience
The RN, because the patient is unstable with potentially life-threatening bleeding
rationale: Unstable patients with changing, unpredictable conditions require RN assessment and management. Experience does not expand LPN scope, UAP monitoring cannot substitute for assessment, and new graduates need stable assignments with support.

stem: A newly licensed RN is starting her third week on the medical-surgical unit with a preceptor. Which assignment is most appropriate?
options: Three stable patients with predictable outcomes, with the preceptor available
Five patients including one with new-onset atrial fibrillation
Charge nurse duties to build leadership skills
Independent care of a patient on a heparin infusion
rationale: New graduates need assignments matched to their developing competency: stable patients, manageable numbers, and preceptor availability. Unstable patients, titratable infusions, and charge duties exceed safe beginning practice.

stem: Which patient group is the best assignment for the LPN on a medical-surgical unit?
options: New admissions with undifferentiated abdominal pain
Patients requiring titration of vasoactive infusions
A patient with sudden respiratory distress
Stable post-op day 3 patients needing routine medications, dressing changes, and data collection
rationale: LPNs provide safe, effective care for stable patients with predictable outcomes, including routine meds, dressing changes, and data collection. New undifferentiated admissions, titrations, and acute deterioration require RN practice.

stem: A medical-surgical RN is floated to the ICU for the first time. The ICU needs help. What is the safest approach?
options: Refuse the float outright because ICUs are unfamiliar
Take a full assignment of ventilated patients independently
Accept a modified assignment of stable ICU patients with an ICU RN buddy resource
Perform only UAP tasks to avoid any risk
rationale: Float nurses should receive assignments within their competency, with orientation to the unit and a resource nurse. Refusing outright is unnecessary when a modified assignment is safe, but independent ventilator management exceeds the float nurse's competency.

stem: An experienced medical-surgical RN is floated to the emergency department. Which assignment is inappropriate?
options: Caring for stable admitted patients boarding in the ED
Triage of incoming patients as the sole triage nurse
Assisting with procedures under ED RN direction
Performing reassessments on stable ED patients
rationale: Triage requires specialized ED competency in rapid assessment and prioritization across undifferentiated patients. A floated nurse without ED experience should take stable, defined assignments rather than independent triage.

stem: The charge nurse notices an RN has slurred speech and smells of alcohol while caring for patients. What is the charge nurse's first action?
options: Confront the RN loudly at the nurses' station
Ensure patient safety by removing the RN from patient care and notifying the supervisor
Ignore it until the end of the shift to avoid conflict
Assign the RN only stable patients for the rest of the shift
rationale: Patient safety comes first: the possibly impaired nurse must be removed from patient care immediately, with coverage arranged and the supervisor notified per policy. Public confrontation and ignoring the situation both endanger patients.

stem: An RN believes her assignment is unsafe due to high acuity and inadequate staffing. What should she do?
options: Abandon the assignment and leave the unit immediately
Accept it silently to avoid being seen as difficult
Refuse all patient care for the shift
Notify the charge nurse, request a modified assignment, document the concern, and follow the chain of command
rationale: The RN should advocate through proper channels: communicate the concern, seek modification, document objectively, and escalate up the chain of command. Abandoning patients or silently accepting an unsafe assignment both violate professional obligations.

stem: Which task is a primary responsibility of the charge nurse at the start of the shift?
options: Making patient assignments based on acuity and staff competency
Administering all scheduled medications for the unit
Performing every admission assessment
Completing all discharge teaching
rationale: The charge nurse's core role is coordinating care: matching patient acuity to staff competency through assignments, overseeing flow, and serving as a resource. Direct-care tasks like all medications or admissions belong to the assigned nurses.

stem: Which scenario constitutes patient abandonment?
options: An RN leaves the unit mid-shift without notifying anyone or handing off her patients
An RN calls in sick four hours before her shift
An RN transfers care to the oncoming nurse with a full report
An RN asks the charge nurse for a modified assignment
rationale: Abandonment is leaving an accepted assignment without arranging continuity of care. Calling in sick before a shift, proper handoff, and requesting modification through channels are all appropriate professional behaviors.

stem: Mid-shift, a patient's nurse is pulled to another unit. What must happen before she leaves?
options: A quick note left at the nurses' station
A text message to the charge nurse
A structured handoff report to the receiving nurse covering status, risks, and pending tasks
Nothing, because the chart contains everything
rationale: Any transfer of responsibility requires direct, structured handoff communication so the receiving nurse understands the patient's status and pending needs. The chart supplements but never replaces verbal handoff.

stem: Four patients need assignment and one RN is the most experienced nurse on the team. Which patient should she take?
options: The stable post-op day 2 patient awaiting discharge
The patient with diabetic ketoacidosis on an insulin infusion with fluctuating glucose
The stable COPD patient on routine nebulizers
The patient admitted for observation with normal vital signs
rationale: The most experienced RN should take the highest-acuity, least predictable patient. DKA on an insulin infusion requires complex assessment and titration, while the stable patients are appropriate for other team members.

stem: The charge nurse is building the UAP's assignment. Which set of tasks is appropriate?
options: Initial assessments on new admissions
Vital signs and ambulation for stable patients, plus intake and output measurement
Blood glucose interpretation and insulin decisions
Sterile dressing changes
rationale: UAP assignments should group routine, predictable tasks for stable patients: vital signs, ADLs, ambulation, and intake and output. Assessments, clinical decisions, and wound care are outside UAP scope.

stem: An unstable GI bleed patient needs close monitoring, and the unit is short-staffed. Which team approach is safest?
options: Assign the patient to the LPN alone to free the RN
Assign the UAP to monitor the patient independently
Pair the LPN with the RN so the RN directs assessment and interventions while the LPN assists with tasks
Leave the patient unassigned until staffing improves
rationale: Team nursing lets the RN retain assessment and decision-making for the unstable patient while the LPN contributes within scope. Assigning the unstable patient to the LPN alone or to a UAP is unsafe.

stem: A travel RN is starting her first shift on the unit. What should the charge nurse do first?
options: Verify her competency and unit orientation, then pair her with a staff nurse resource
Give her the heaviest assignment to test her skills
Assign her charge duties since she is experienced
Let her choose whichever patients she prefers
rationale: Agency and travel nurses need competency verification, unit orientation, and a resource nurse, even when experienced. Assignments should be within verified competency, not used as tests or based on preference alone.

stem: Two nursing assistants are arguing loudly at the nurses' station about task assignments. What should the charge nurse do first?
options: Ignore it since it does not involve patients
Intervene promptly and move the discussion to a private area to resolve it
Reprimand both in front of the team as a deterrent
Immediately terminate both employees
rationale: The charge nurse must address disruptive behavior promptly and privately to maintain a professional environment. Public shaming and ignoring the conflict both harm team function; termination is a management decision, not a charge nurse's first step.

stem: A family member complains that his mother's pain is not being managed. What is the charge nurse's best response?
options: Listen to the concern, assess the patient's pain with the assigned nurse, and follow up on the plan
Tell the family the nurse knows best
Promise the family a specific medication dose
Document the complaint without investigating
rationale: The charge nurse should acknowledge the concern, directly assess the situation with the assigned nurse, ensure the pain plan is addressed, and follow up. Dismissing the family or promising specific orders is inappropriate.

stem: A rapid response team is being formed for a deteriorating patient. Who should lead the bedside response?
options: The UAP, who knows the patient's routine
The LPN, working independently
The patient's RN, coordinating with the responding team using assessment findings
The first available staff member regardless of role
rationale: The primary RN leads with assessment data and knowledge of the patient's baseline, coordinating with the response team. Others contribute within their roles, but clinical leadership requires the RN's assessment.

stem: During a code blue on the unit, what is the charge nurse's most important role?
options: Perform all code interventions personally
Leave the unit to call the family
Coordinate roles, ensure the code cart and team are in place, and maintain unit coverage
Document every detail while others work
rationale: The charge nurse coordinates the response: assigning roles, ensuring equipment, and keeping the rest of the unit covered. Doing everything personally or abandoning coordination weakens the response.

stem: The unit census suddenly rises with three new admissions and no additional staff yet. What should the charge nurse do first?
options: Prioritize patient safety: triage admissions by acuity, redistribute tasks, and activate the call-in process
Refuse all admissions until staffing is ideal
Assign all new admissions to the UAP
Cancel all staff breaks for the shift
rationale: The charge nurse manages surges by acuity-based triage, redistribution, and following the escalation and call-in policy. Refusing admissions outright or assigning them unsafely violates the duty to provide care.

stem: How should the charge nurse manage meal breaks on a busy shift?
options: Let everyone take breaks at the same time
Stagger breaks with clear coverage assignments so no patient is left without a responsible nurse
Skip breaks when the unit is busy
Leave break coverage to chance
rationale: Patient care must be continuous; the charge nurse staggers breaks and designates coverage for each nurse's patients. Simultaneous breaks or skipped coverage create unsafe gaps.

stem: A nursing student is assigned to the unit. Who is responsible for the student's patients?
options: The student, who is independently responsible
The nursing instructor, who is off-site
The UAP, who works alongside the student
The RN preceptor, who supervises and retains accountability for delegated student activities
rationale: The supervising RN retains accountability for patients when delegating activities to a student, providing direction and supervision. Students practice under supervision and are not independent practitioners.

stem: A preceptor is working with a new graduate. Which preceptor action best supports safe practice?
options: Let the new nurse manage everything independently from day one
Gradually increase the new nurse's independence while directly supervising high-risk tasks
Perform all tasks for the new nurse to prevent errors
Evaluate the new nurse only at the end of orientation
rationale: Effective precepting scaffolds independence: direct supervision for high-risk tasks, graduated responsibility, and ongoing feedback. Total independence too early and doing everything for the orientee both prevent safe competency development.

stem: When making assignments, why should the charge nurse consider giving nurses the same patients on consecutive shifts?
options: It reduces the need for handoff reports
Continuity improves the nurse's knowledge of the patient and detects subtle changes earlier
It guarantees the patient will prefer that nurse
It eliminates the need for care plans
rationale: Continuity of caregiver strengthens assessment through familiarity with baselines and trends. Handoff is still required every shift, and care plans remain essential.

stem: An RN is told she must work a double shift after already working 12 hours and feels too fatigued to be safe. What should she do?
options: Communicate her fatigue-related safety concern up the chain of command and request relief
Work the shift silently despite feeling unsafe
Leave without telling anyone
Take a stimulant to get through the shift
rationale: Fatigue impairs judgment and endangers patients; the nurse must voice the safety concern through proper channels and seek alternatives. Silent compliance, abandonment, and self-medicating are all unsafe.

stem: A nurse is floated to a unit where she believes she lacks competency for the assigned patients. What is her best action?
options: Refuse to enter the unit
Accept the float but request a modified assignment within her competency, with orientation and a resource nurse
Accept the full assignment without question
Trade all her patients to the UAP
rationale: The nurse should not refuse the float outright nor accept an unsafe assignment. The professional approach is to disclose competency limits and negotiate a safe, modified assignment with support.

stem: A medication error occurred on the unit. What is the charge nurse's role in the immediate follow-up?
options: Determine who to punish
Hide the error to protect the unit's reputation
Decide the nurse's employment fate
Ensure the patient is safe, gather objective facts, and support completion of the incident report
rationale: The charge nurse's immediate role is patient safety and objective fact-gathering for the incident report and system learning. Blame and employment decisions belong to management through a just-culture process.

stem: A nurse has unfinished nonurgent tasks at shift change. What should she do?
options: Leave without mentioning them
Stay four extra hours to finish everything
Document them as completed
Give a complete handoff including pending tasks so the oncoming nurse can prioritize them
rationale: Safe handoff includes pending tasks so nothing is lost between shifts. Falsifying completion or omitting tasks endangers the patient; staying excessively long creates fatigue risks.

stem: An on-call nurse is called in for a surge but reports she has been drinking at a family event. What should the supervisor do?
options: Have her come in anyway because the need is urgent
Excuse her from duty and call the next nurse, since impaired staff cannot provide safe care
Assign her only documentation tasks
Tell her to drink coffee on the way
rationale: Fitness for duty is nonnegotiable; an impaired nurse must not provide patient care. The supervisor moves to the next call-in option rather than compromising safety.

stem: Why should the charge nurse perform regular rounds on all patients during the shift?
options: To take over all patient care
To audit nurses for punishment
To replace hourly rounding by assistants
To identify safety risks, verify care is on track, and support bedside nurses
rationale: Charge rounds provide oversight: catching risks, confirming priorities, and offering help. They supplement rather than replace the assigned nurse's care and are not punitive audits.

stem: A newly licensed LPN joins the unit. Which assignment approach is safest?
options: Stable patients with predictable outcomes, paired with an experienced nurse mentor
A full independent assignment including unstable patients
Charge nurse responsibilities to learn quickly
Only UAP-level tasks indefinitely
rationale: New LPN graduates need stable, predictable assignments with mentorship while they build competency. Unstable patients and charge duties exceed beginning LPN practice, while restricting them to UAP tasks wastes their licensed scope.

stem: A telemetry RN is floated to another telemetry unit. Which assignment is most appropriate?
options: The ICU ventilator patients
Independent triage in the ED
No patients, only observation
A standard telemetry assignment after brief unit orientation
rationale: Floating to a similar unit with the same patient population is the safest float scenario. A brief orientation to unit specifics plus a standard assignment within competency is appropriate.

stem: In primary nursing, what distinguishes the primary RN's role?
options: The primary RN does every task without help
The primary RN owns the 24-hour care plan and accountability for outcomes
Associate nurses make all the decisions
The primary RN works every shift
rationale: Primary nursing gives one RN accountability for planning and outcomes across the stay, with associate nurses implementing the plan on other shifts. It is about accountability and planning, not physical presence around the clock.

stem: A patient with a history of aggression toward staff needs assignment. Who should take this patient?
options: The new graduate RN, to build confidence
The UAP, for 1:1 observation alone
The LPN, without informing her of the history
An experienced RN skilled in de-escalation, with a safety plan and backup available
rationale: Potentially violent patients require experienced RN assessment, de-escalation skill, and safety planning. Withholding the history or assigning inexperienced staff alone endangers the team.

stem: A newly admitted patient speaks only Mandarin and needs complex discharge teaching. Which assignment consideration matters most?
options: Assign an RN and arrange a qualified medical interpreter for assessment and teaching
Assign the UAP, who speaks some Mandarin
Use a bilingual family member's child as interpreter
Skip the teaching since it is too difficult
rationale: Accurate assessment and teaching require a qualified medical interpreter, not ad hoc bilingual staff or children. The RN leads the teaching with proper interpretation to ensure understanding.

stem: Three patients on the unit have C. difficile. How should the charge nurse assign their care?
options: Cohort the infected patients with the same nurses when possible to limit cross-contamination
Assign each infected patient to a different nurse to share the load
Assign all infected patients to the UAP
Mix infected and noninfected patients for fairness
rationale: Cohorting infected patients with the same staff reduces transmission risk. Spreading them across all staff or mixing assignments increases exposure, and UAP-only assignment ignores acuity needs.

stem: One nurse called in sick and no replacement is available. What is the charge nurse's priority?
options: Give all the sick nurse's patients to the UAP
Redistribute the assignment by acuity, ensure the highest-risk patients have RN coverage, and escalate
Close the unit to new admissions permanently
Tell nurses to work faster
rationale: The charge nurse protects the highest-acuity patients first, redistributes safely, and escalates through the chain of command. Dumping patients on the UAP or demanding speed compromises safety.

stem: An experienced LPN asks to take the unstable GI bleed patient because the RNs are busy. How should the charge nurse respond?
options: Agree, since the LPN is experienced
Let the LPN try it for an hour
Decline and keep the unstable patient with an RN, offering the LPN additional stable patients instead
Assign the patient to the UAP instead
rationale: Instability requires RN assessment regardless of LPN experience. The charge nurse protects scope boundaries while using the LPN fully within scope on stable patients.

stem: A new graduate RN asks to take the patient with new-onset atrial fibrillation and hypotension for the experience. What should the preceptor do?
options: Assign the patient to the new nurse alone
Refuse to let the new nurse near the patient
Keep the unstable patient with the preceptor and involve the new nurse in supervised learning
Send the new nurse home
rationale: The preceptor balances learning with safety: the new nurse observes and assists under direct supervision while the preceptor retains the unstable assignment. Solo assignment is unsafe; total exclusion wastes a learning opportunity.

stem: The charge nurse sees a colleague preparing to administer a medication without checking the patient's identification. What should she do first?
options: Say nothing to avoid embarrassing the colleague
Intervene immediately to stop the error, then address it privately and follow up per policy
Report it to the state board immediately
Announce the mistake to the whole unit
rationale: Immediate intervention prevents patient harm; the follow-up conversation happens privately and respectfully, with reporting per policy. Public shaming and immediate board reporting skip the proper just-culture process.

stem: An RN arrives with a fever and productive cough during flu season. What should the charge nurse do?
options: Let her work with a mask on a full assignment
Assign her only to immunocompromised patients
Send her home per infection-control policy and arrange coverage
Ignore it because staffing is short
rationale: Infection-control policy and patient safety require ill staff with febrile respiratory symptoms to be excluded from patient care. Short staffing does not override the duty to protect patients.

stem: How should the charge nurse's own patient assignment be structured?
options: The heaviest assignment, since she is the most experienced
No patients at all on any unit
The same load as every other nurse
A lighter or flexible assignment so she can fulfill coordination and resource duties
rationale: The charge role requires availability for admissions, emergencies, and staff support, so the assignment should be light or flexible. A full heavy load prevents the charge nurse from performing coordination duties.

stem: At 2 AM the night charge nurse faces an unsafe staffing situation. Who should she contact?
options: No one, since managers are asleep
The day shift charge nurse at home
The media
The house supervisor or administrator on call, following the chain of command
rationale: The chain of command operates around the clock through the house supervisor. The night charge nurse must escalate unsafe conditions rather than managing them silently.

stem: A patient boarding in the ED for 8 hours is still under ED care. The floor has an open bed but no available RN. What is the safest plan?
options: Move the patient to the floor hallway without an assigned nurse
Have the UAP transport and monitor the patient alone on the floor
Discharge the patient to free the ED bed
Keep the patient in the ED with ED nursing coverage until the floor can safely accept handoff
rationale: Patients must move with appropriate nursing coverage and handoff. Moving a patient to an uncovered floor bed or leaving monitoring to a UAP alone is unsafe; throughput pressure never justifies uncovered care.

stem: After a difficult code, several nurses are distressed. What should the charge nurse do?
options: Tell everyone to get back to work immediately
Assign blame for the outcome
Cancel all future debriefs to save time
Facilitate a debrief covering what went well, what to improve, and staff support resources
rationale: Structured debriefing supports learning and staff wellbeing after critical events. Skipping it or turning it into blame misses the safety and resilience benefits.

stem: Before a new graduate takes an independent assignment, what must the preceptor confirm?
options: That the new nurse has demonstrated competency in the required skills and judgments
That orientation hours are complete regardless of performance
That the new nurse feels confident
That the unit needs the staffing
rationale: Progression to independence requires demonstrated competency, not just completed hours or self-confidence. Staffing needs never justify advancing an unready nurse.

stem: A UAP is floated to another medical-surgical unit. Which assignment is appropriate?
options: Sterile dressing changes, since the unit is busy
Independent patient assessments
Routine tasks within her validated competency, such as vital signs and ADLs on stable patients
Medication administration
rationale: Floating does not expand UAP scope. The floated UAP takes routine tasks within validated competency on stable patients, with orientation to the unit's routines.

stem: A float RN arrives on the unit. What is the charge nurse's responsibility?
options: Give her the assignment and leave her alone
Assume she knows everything from her home unit
Assign her only to answer call lights
Provide unit orientation covering layout, emergency equipment, documentation, and introduce a resource nurse
rationale: The charge nurse must orient float nurses to unit-specific systems and provide a resource contact. Assuming competence with local systems or isolating the float nurse is unsafe.

stem: A nurse becomes ill mid-shift and must leave. What should the charge nurse do?
options: Tell her to stay until the shift ends
Leave her patients uncovered until the next shift
Arrange handoff of her patients to covering nurses and redistribute by acuity
Give all her patients to the UAP
rationale: Illness mid-shift requires prompt handoff and acuity-based redistribution with coverage. Forcing the ill nurse to stay or leaving patients uncovered endangers everyone.

stem: When staffing is tight, what ethical principle should guide the charge nurse's assignment decisions?
options: Seniority privileges for preferred assignments
Minimizing overtime costs above all
Patient safety and equitable care take priority over convenience or speed
Keeping the charge nurse's own workload lightest
rationale: Assignments must serve patient safety and fairness first. Cost, convenience, and favoritism are secondary to the duty to provide safe, equitable care.

stem: The unit has two RNs, two LPNs, and two UAPs for 18 patients of mixed acuity. What is the charge nurse's best approach?
options: Divide patients evenly with three per staff member regardless of role
Assign RNs to the highest-acuity patients and assessments, LPNs to stable patients, UAPs to routine tasks
Give all patients to the RNs and use others for errands
Assign by room number proximity only
rationale: Effective skill mix matches role scope to patient need: RNs for high acuity and assessments, LPNs for stable patients, UAPs for routine tasks. Even splits ignore scope and acuity.

stem: One RN consistently receives the heaviest assignments. What should the charge nurse do?
options: Continue the pattern since she handles it well
Track assignment acuity over time and balance the load fairly among staff
Give her lighter patients as a reward instead of balance
Ignore it because assignments are random
rationale: Fairness requires the charge nurse to monitor acuity distribution and balance assignments over time. Consistently overloading the most capable nurse leads to burnout and errors.

stem: The charge nurse notices an RN has delegated assessments to the UAP. What should she do?
options: Intervene, educate on delegation boundaries, and ensure the assessments are completed by licensed staff
Praise the RN's efficiency
Document the UAP's assessment skills
Reassign the RN to a different unit
rationale: The charge nurse must correct unsafe delegation immediately and use it as a teaching moment. Assessments cannot be delegated to UAPs, and the patients still need proper assessment.

stem: Three admissions arrive at once. How should the charge nurse distribute them?
options: Assign based on acuity and nurse competency, staggering starts so each admission gets a safe assessment
Give all three to the newest nurse
Assign them to whoever is closest to the door
Delay all admissions for two hours
rationale: Acuity-based distribution with staggered starts keeps admissions safe. Dumping admissions on one nurse or delaying needed care without clinical reason is unsafe.

stem: The UAP reports she cannot complete vital signs for ten patients safely. What should the charge nurse do?
options: Reassess the workload, redistribute tasks, and ensure the assignment is achievable
Tell her to work faster
Write her up for complaining
Add more patients to motivate her
rationale: An overloaded delegatee is a safety risk. The charge nurse must rebalance the work and verify tasks are achievable within the shift, not punish the report.

stem: The assigned RN is pulled to a rapid response, leaving her patients covered by the LPN. What must the charge nurse ensure?
options: That the LPN takes over all RN duties
That the patients wait until the RN returns
That the LPN's coverage stays within scope and an RN remains available for assessments
That the UAP assumes the RN's patients
rationale: Coverage during emergencies must respect scope: the LPN handles routine tasks while RN assessment responsibility is explicitly covered by another RN. Scope does not expand because of an emergency.

stem: A preceptor and new nurse disagree about the care plan. What should the charge nurse do?
options: Side with whoever is louder
Remove the new nurse from the unit
Facilitate a discussion focused on evidence and patient safety, with the preceptor retaining final accountability
Let them resolve it without guidance
rationale: The charge nurse mediates by grounding the discussion in evidence and safety, while clarifying that the preceptor holds accountability for the patient. Unstructured conflict risks both safety and learning.

stem: A patient requests a nurse of a specific gender for personal care. How should the charge nurse respond?
options: Accommodate the request when staffing allows, balancing patient dignity with fair assignments
Refuse all such requests on principle
Grant every request regardless of staffing impact
Ask the UAP to handle it instead
rationale: Reasonable accommodation of dignity-related requests is appropriate when feasible, balanced against staffing realities. Blanket refusals ignore patient dignity; automatic grants ignore safety and fairness.

stem: A patient is actively dying and the family needs extensive support. Which assignment fits?
options: The UAP alone for the shift
The busiest RN to fit it in
An RN with a lighter overall load to allow time for assessment and family support
The LPN without RN backup
rationale: End-of-life care requires RN assessment of symptoms and skilled family support, which takes time. A lighter load protects the quality of this care; leaving it to unlicensed staff alone is inadequate.

stem: What should the charge nurse document about staffing decisions?
options: Personal opinions about staff competence
Nothing, to avoid liability
Only positive events
Objective notes on acuity, assignments, staffing concerns raised, and actions taken
rationale: Objective documentation of staffing decisions and escalations creates an accurate record and supports safety review. Opinions, omissions, and selective positivity undermine its purpose.

stem: What is the charge nurse's role in interdisciplinary rounds?
options: Cancel rounds when busy
Speak for all disciplines
Skip rounds to pass medications
Coordinate attendance, share nursing assessment priorities, and follow up on the plan
rationale: The charge nurse ensures nursing's assessment and priorities inform the team plan and that follow-up happens. Canceling or skipping rounds fragments care coordination.

stem: Nurses report the current ratios feel unsafe for the acuity. What should the charge nurse do?
options: Validate the concern, assess acuity objectively, and escalate through the chain of command with data
Dismiss the concern as complaining
Tell nurses to stop reporting concerns
Fix it alone without telling management
rationale: The charge nurse takes safety concerns seriously, gathers acuity data, and escalates formally. Dismissing concerns or hiding them from leadership prevents system-level solutions.

stem: A nurse is asked to be charge on a unit where she has never worked. What should she do?
options: Refuse any charge role forever
Accept without orientation to prove herself
Delegate all charge duties to the UAP
Accept only with orientation, a resource nurse, and a manageable patient load
rationale: Charge competency is unit-specific; accepting requires orientation and support. Refusing all future charge roles is unnecessary, but accepting blindly or delegating charge duties to unlicensed staff is unsafe.

stem: When assigning a complex wound-care patient, which nurse factor matters most?
options: Demonstrated competency in wound assessment and management
Seniority on the unit
Personal preference for wounds
Whoever has the fewest patients regardless of skill
rationale: Assignments should match demonstrated competency to patient need. Seniority and preference do not equal skill, and low census alone does not qualify a nurse for complex care.

stem: A patient asks for a different nurse, citing a personality clash. What should the charge nurse do?
options: Refuse and tell the patient to adapt
Explore the concern, assess for safety issues, and reassign if feasible without punishing either party
Immediately discipline the assigned nurse
Grant it without asking any questions
rationale: The charge nurse investigates to rule out safety or conduct issues, then accommodates when feasible. Automatic refusal ignores the therapeutic relationship; automatic discipline skips due process.

stem: How can the charge nurse prevent one nurse from getting all the total-care patients?
options: Assign total-care patients alphabetically
Distribute high-workload patients across the team and rotate heavy assignments over time
Give them all to the strongest nurse every day
Leave it to luck
rationale: Intentional distribution and rotation of heavy assignments protect fairness and prevent burnout. Alphabetical or luck-based assignment ignores workload equity.
